title: What Stress Does to Your Body (December Edition)
description:
What stress does to your body, December edition. Cyto swears he's too chill to get stressed, but the alarm at Queen's Park HQ won't stop: Mito plays a pickup game against THE ALARM, Officer Neutro writes up four incident reports (exams, a 43-person Secret Santa group chat, the mall, your auntie), and Rhino the cold virus plans a heist through your nose. Then the cold case from 1991 that had Cyto going "bro, what", a twist nobody saw coming, and three cheat codes to shut the alarm off before the break.

Quick version: when your brain sees stress it hits the alarm, the adrenal glands on top of your kidneys pump out adrenaline and cortisol, and your heart rate, breathing and blood sugar go up (fight or flight). A little is useful. Days and days of it is where it gets weird: researchers at Carnegie Mellon found long-running stress can make immune cells stop listening to cortisol, so inflammation doesn't shut off properly. In a 1991 study of about 400 volunteers who had cold viruses dripped into their noses, infection went from about 74% (low stress) to about 90% (high stress), and actual colds from 27% to 47%. Some studies find more heart attacks around Christmas and New Year's (not every study): if someone has chest pain over the holidays, don't wait it out, call 911.

Cheat codes: 1) slow your breathing (in a 12-week trial anxiety dropped; a longer exhale didn't matter, slow did), 2) pick your side quest (exercise, meditation and slow-breathing training lowered stress about the same over 5 weeks), 3) mute the group chat for a bit, say no to one thing, protect your sleep. Skate at Nathan Phillips Square, walk the Distillery Winter Village (free before 4 pm), or just walk the block.

Sources:
Fight-or-flight (stress -> brain -> adrenal glands -> adrenaline + cortisol; heart rate, breathing, blood sugar up): standard physiology textbook.
Cohen S, et al. PNAS 2012 (glucocorticoid receptor resistance, inflammation, colds; Carnegie Mellon) — https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1118355109
Cohen S, Tyrrell DAJ, Smith AP. NEJM 1991 (psychological stress and susceptibility to the common cold, 394 volunteers) — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199108293250903
Kloner RA. Progress in Cardiovascular Diseases 2006 (holiday-season cardiac events) — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pcad.2005.07.001
Milne EMG. European Journal of Epidemiology 2005 (New Year, not Christmas, spike; NE England) — https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-005-2147-8
Weerasinghe DP, et al. Heart 2002 (no holiday increase; NSW) — https://doi.org/10.1136/heart.88.1.30
Birdee G, et al. Complementary Therapies in Medicine 2023 (12-week slow-breathing RCT) — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ctim.2023.102937
van der Zwan JE, et al. Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback 2015 (exercise vs meditation vs HRV-biofeedback breathing) — https://doi.org/10.1007/s10484-015-9293-x
Distillery Winter Village (free before 4 pm; ticketed from 4 pm on peak dates) — thedistillerywintervillage.com
Nathan Phillips Square skating — City of Toronto (toronto.ca)

Not medical advice. If you or someone you know has chest pain, call 911.
